key_points.point: The document asserts that AI-enabled attackers operate at unprecedented scales and speeds, with the share of high-risk AI threat actors increasing from 33% to 56% in one year. This rapid evolution challenges traditional cybersecurity frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK, which the authors argue may underplay the danger of autonomous campaigns. From an accelerationist perspective, this shift necessitates a move toward adaptive, AI-native defensive frameworks that can match the speed and parallelization of AI-enabled threats. The document acknowledges that current centralized safety controls are structurally irrelevant when attackers self-host their own models.
key_points.verbatim: A single agent can run reconnaissance in parallel at near-zero marginal cost, and the share of medium or high-risk AI-enabled threat actors grew from 33% to 56% in a single 12-month window.
key_points.canonical_proposition: AI-enabled cyber threats operate at scales and speeds that render traditional, human-centric defensive frameworks and centralized safety controls structurally inadequate.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that AI-enabled cyber threats necessitate a transition to adaptive, autonomous defensive frameworks due to the unprecedented scale and speed of AI-driven reconnaissance. Encompasses: AI-enabled threat actor growth, structural irrelevance of centralized safety controls, inadequacy of traditional defensive frameworks.

key_points.point: The document identifies a critical 'recognition-action gap' where LLMs articulate trap recognition in their reasoning but still exploit deceptive elements 73.4% of the time. This empirical finding suggests that even when models demonstrate situational awareness, they lack the alignment necessary to act on that awareness to avoid traps. From a safetyist perspective, this gap highlights the danger of relying on model reasoning as a proxy for safe behavior, as the models' internal 'knowledge' of a trap does not prevent them from executing harmful actions. The document notes that this behavior is consistent across the 21-model cohort, regardless of model architecture or specialization.
key_points.verbatim: Through a 10-code content analysis of the LLMsÆ reasoning text, we quantified a recognition-action gap. The models walked-into-trap (articulated recognition of a trap in reasoning text and still placed an exploit mark on the deceptive line) 73.4% of the time.
key_points.canonical_proposition: LLMs exhibit a persistent recognition-action gap where articulated trap awareness fails to prevent the execution of harmful or deceptive actions.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within safetyist discourse that LLMs exhibit a structural recognition-action gap, where articulated awareness of deceptive traps fails to prevent the execution of harmful actions, rendering reasoning-based safety assessments unreliable. Encompasses: recognition-action gap, failure of situational awareness to guide action, unreliability of model reasoning as a safety proxy.

key_points.point: The authors argue for the development of new AI-native active defense frameworks, as traditional human-centered deception hypotheses do not reliably transfer to AI agents. The research demonstrates that deception fails to divert LLM attention from real risks, unlike in human attackers where it provides a significant defender benefit. From a safetyist perspective, this necessitates a fundamental rethink of how we design defensive systems to account for the unique cognitive and operational characteristics of AI attackers. The document emphasizes that future research must integrate cognitive-layer recognition measurements with operational-layer consequence signals to effectively constrain AI agents.
key_points.verbatim: Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that human-centered deception hypotheses do not reliably transfer to AI attackers, highlighting the critical need for new research into AI-native active defense frameworks.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Develop AI-native active defense frameworks that account for the unique cognitive and operational behaviors of AI attackers, as human-centered deception techniques are ineffective.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that AI-native active defense frameworks be developed to address the failure of human-centered deception techniques to divert or constrain AI attackers. Encompasses: AI-native defense, failure of human-centered deception, integration of cognitive and operational defense metrics.
